claims.arxiv2606_24026: Language-model agents can be useful explainers of transformer circuits that have already been located for them, both by saying what each component does and by saying what the circuit computes as a whole. Useful means at least one agent classifies more than half of the components correctly, scores above 0.50 on a 0-to-1 scale for the quality of its written role descriptions, where 0, 0.5 and 1 stand for wrong, partly right and right, and names the overall task correctly for more than half the circuits. Because the circuit is handed over in advance, this is about explanation after localisation, not about finding circuits.
claims.arxiv2606_24026_c1: For agents explaining circuits that have already been located, imposing a staged workflow of observe, hypothesise, then test causally produces better explanations than either cutting a stage out of that workflow or letting an equally capable agent work however it likes with the same tools. Counts as better than the cut-down versions only if it gives strictly higher circuit-level task accuracy for every model when each stage is removed in turn, and wins more than half the resulting component-level comparisons. Counts as better than unrestricted tool use only if both component classification and role-description quality are strictly higher while circuit-level task accuracy is no lower.
claims.arxiv2606_24026_c2: When these agents fail at explaining a located circuit, the failure sits in testing the hypothesis rather than in forming it. Hypotheses count as mostly grounded in what the agent observed if their mean human grounding score is above 1 on a 0-to-2 scale, where 0 is unsupported, 1 partly supported and 2 fully supported. Testing is the bottleneck if the plans for testing average below both that grounding score and the fully sound score of 2, if code written to run those tests fails some of the time, and if components are still unresolved once the iteration budget runs out. The attribution additionally requires that the agent with the fewest unresolved components also has the highest final component accuracy, and the one with the most has the lowest final scores.

0.text: Build a benchmark where the right answer is known. Setup: start from 84 small transformers compiled from symbolic programs, each with its circuit already located, dropping two tasks whose circuits are famous enough that a model might recall them. Trace each located component back through the compilation map to the program variable it implements, and annotate every component by hand with a free-text note and one of five functional tags. Give each task its program, a ground-truth description and five input-output examples produced by running it. Result: 84 circuits and 163 components (120 MLP, 43 attention), unevenly spread across the five tags, averaging 1.94 components per circuit and ranging from 1 to 10.

1.text: Fix the agent's procedure and budget. Setup: for each supplied component, the agent observes, proposes a hypothesis and tests it causally, with the five-tag vocabulary withheld until a later classification step; after all components it assigns tags and notes and infers the circuit's task from its own validated hypotheses plus the examples. Code may use provided helper libraries or be written from scratch, with up to five execution attempts per stage and at most three hypothesis-test rounds per component; an unsupported hypothesis is kept as tentative. Measured: exact tag accuracy, role-description quality rescaled to 0/0.5/1, binary task-description accuracy, and the share of code executions that run without error.

2.text: Check the automated scoring against people. Setup: two human judges independently score anonymised, shuffled outputs on the same rubrics, taking the lower of their two scores, which matches how the two model judges are combined. Result: on a cross-model subset, human-human agreement is kappa 0.83 for role quality and 0.96 for task accuracy, and the lower human score against the lower model-judge score agrees at 0.76 and 0.80. On a larger subset the figures are 0.80/0.96 and 0.75/0.86. Scoring of the test plans is much less reliable, with human-human kappa of 0.37 and 0.46, so the authors keep it as a diagnostic rather than an official metric.

3.text: Can the agents explain located circuits? Setup: run the full workflow over all 84 circuits and 163 components with four different model backbones. Result: tag accuracy 0.74, 0.79, 0.76 and 0.67; role-description quality 0.46, 0.58, 0.59 and 0.25; task accuracy 0.63, 0.75, 0.83 and 0.25; code-execution success 0.52, 0.93, 0.80 and 0.62. Three of the four clear all three bars; the weakest clears only the component-classification one. No backbone is best on every metric: one leads on component tags, another on role and task quality.

4.text: Are the hypotheses actually supported by what the agent saw? Setup: on a 10-task, 17-component subset, score every observation-hypothesis pair by hand from 0 (contradicts or ignores the observation) to 2 (fully supported). Result: the three stronger backbones average 1.94, with a single partly supported hypothesis and none ungrounded. The weakest averages 1.41, fully grounding only 41.2% of cases, typically starting from a generically true observation and then adding task-specific mechanism it has no evidence for.

5.text: Would the proposed test actually test the hypothesis? Setup: on the same subset, human annotators score the test plans from 0 (no meaningful test) through 1 (indirect or partial) to 2 (fully tests the hypothesis), taking the lower annotator score. Result: 1.71, 1.41, 1.24 and 0.71 across the four backbones, all below the grounding scores and all below 2. The rating judges the proposed experiment only, not whether the hypothesis is right or the code runs.

6.text: What stops the tests producing usable evidence? Setup: cluster the failed code executions by error type across the four backbones, using 314, 101, 191 and 301 failures respectively. Result: the categories are tensor and Python bugs, library misuse, runtime-environment errors, lookup errors, off-by-one and position-offset mistakes, and protocol failures such as omitting the required result variable. These sit alongside execution success rates of 0.52, 0.93, 0.80 and 0.62.

7.text: Does finishing the test loop predict a good final explanation? Setup: count components whose hypothesis is supported on the first, second or third round and those still unresolved when the three-round budget runs out. Result: the strongest backbone resolves 106 on the first hypothesis, 32 on the second and 8 on the third, leaving 17 unresolved; another leaves 38; the weakest leaves 57. The one with the fewest unresolved components also has the highest tag accuracy, and the one with the most has the lowest final scores.

8.text: Does each stage of the workflow earn its place? Setup: on the full benchmark, compare the whole workflow with one version that drops the dedicated observation stage and one that sends the first hypothesis straight to classification without testing it. Result: the full workflow has the highest task accuracy for every backbone, with removal of either stage costing 1 to 18 percentage points, and higher component-level scores in 14 of 16 comparisons. Both exceptions are on the weakest backbone, where dropping a stage slightly helps.

9.text: Is the structure doing the work, or just the tools? Setup: run the workflow and an unconstrained coding agent on the same 31-task, 55-component subset with the same model and the same evaluation context, the difference being that the unconstrained agent need not follow the staged procedure. Result: the workflow scores 0.811 tag accuracy, 0.639 role quality, 0.767 task accuracy and 0.94 execution success, against 0.770, 0.603, 0.767 and 0.69. Task accuracy is identical, so the gain is on the component-level metrics. Inspection shows the unconstrained agent performs a causal intervention in only 15 of 31 cases, relies on observation alone in 12, and infers the task from the examples without loading the model at all in 4.

10.text: Is the ranking of backbones an artefact of the judges or of one lucky run? Setup: score role and task descriptions with each of the two model judges separately rather than only in combination, and repeat runs on a fixed subset. Result: both judges give the same ranking on task accuracy; on role quality both place the same two backbones third and fourth while the top two swap, separated by a small margin. No judge favours its own model family, and repeated runs preserve the backbone-level pattern.

notes: The last quarter of the paper, an appendix case study on a circuit in a real 8B model, belongs to a thin claim that was not kept, so nothing needed from it. [3] now states which bars each backbone clears, [8] which comparisons the two exceptions come from, and [9] that task accuracy ties, which is exactly the clause C1's bar turns on.
